summary:
We developed Mars Outpost Survival (missionmars.games), a 2D browser game for ages 7–12 that trains young players in systems thinking, and real NASA science. We built with Phaser 3 for computers, tablets, and phones, the game challenges players to survive 10 sols (Martian days) as a lone astronaut managing a outpost.

To make real space operations engaging and accessible, every storm is scaled by actual space-weather records from NASA’s DONKI database (coronal mass ejections, solar flares, and geomagnetic storms), paired with NASA OSDR-inspired biological events and Martian rover discoveries. Players must balance interdependent Power, Oxygen, and Food budgets, plan around Earth–Mars light-speed communication delays, and deploy targeted engineering defenses before hazards strike.

Mars Outpost Survival is important because it teaches STEM by doing rather than passive reading which shows the next generation of explorers that surviving on Mars depends on advance forecasting, resource trade-offs, and real-world NASA engineering.
details:
How It Works & Core Gameplay: Mars Outpost Survival (missionmars.games) is a 2D browser-based survival and resource-management game designed for ages 7 to 12. Players step into the boots of a lone astronaut tasked with keeping a Martian habitat operational for 10 sols (Mars days).

Each Sol follows a structured mission loop:

  • Morning Briefing (Clock Paused): Players review incoming space-weather alerts at the Comms terminal. Each storm is dynamically scaled using real space-weather records fetched from NASA’s DONKI database (Coronal Mass Ejection speeds in km/s, geomagnetic storm Kp indices, and solar flare classes), complete with the real observation date and a direct link to the NASA archive record.
  • 90-Second Action Phase: Players walk between outpost wings to balance three interdependent resources—Power, Oxygen, and Food where every action has a trade-off:
    • North Wing: Raise Electromagnetic Shielding (−30 Power) before a storm hits, or retract solar panels during dust storms (saving panels at the cost of solar power generation).
    • East Wing: Run Crop Incubators (−20 Power, −15 Oxygen for +30 Food).
    • West Wing: Run the Oxygen Generator (−15 Power for +30 Oxygen).
    • South Wing: Perform EVAs to sweep dust off solar panels (−10 Oxygen for +30 Power), collect rock samples for research (−15 Oxygen), or toggle Dust Scrubbers (−0.1 Power/sec to prevent dust from slowing movement).
    • Command Hub: Request emergency assistance from Earth, which takes 25 seconds to simulate the real 6-to-44-minute Earth–Mars light-speed communication delay.
  • Unwarned Mid-Sol Surprises & Off-Path Exploration: Beyond forecasted storms, players handle multi-step mid-Sol events such as grabbing a patch kit to seal a micrometeoroid hull breach, dodging a dust devil before sweeping panels, hauling cargo from a supply pod, or collecting glowing rock samples. Players can also explore off the paved paths to uncover six hidden Martian discoveries per mission (such as Opportunity’s hematite "blueberries," Curiosity’s sulfur crystals, and Perseverance’s leopard-spot rock), unlocking entries in a persistent 10-page Field Journal.
  • Night Cycle & Engineering Debrief: At night, the base consumes baseline Oxygen, Food, and Power, followed by a summary explaining the real-world scientific constraint behind the day's events. Surviving all 10 sols unlocks a mission debrief detailing how real NASA engineering solutions address the exact hazards the player survived.

Benefits & Intended Impact Mars Outpost Survival shifts STEM education from passive reading to active systems thinking and calm triage. Young players experience firsthand that life support on another planet is a tightly coupled budget—producing food requires both power and oxygen, and defenses only work if deployed before a hazard arrives. By embedding plain-language definitions (sol, CME, Kp index, regolith, hydroponics) directly into gameplay and tying storm intensity to authentic NASA telemetry, the game builds scientific literacy, problem-solving under pressure, and excitement for real space exploration.

Creativity & Design Approach Rather than treating NASA APIs as a background scoreboard, the game translates raw astrophysical measurements into tangible gameplay consequences. High-speed CMEs and severe Kp indices visibly shake the habitat, tint the atmosphere dusty orange, and force players to make split-second triage decisions. Replayability is driven by three difficulty tiers (Cadet, Astronaut, Commander), five randomized landing sites with unique resource modifiers (Sunny Plateau, Garden Dome, Shield Ridge, Dusty Valley, Standard), shuffled storm sequences that intensify by 4% each Sol, and eight collectible achievement badges.

Accessibility & Key Design Considerations

  • Universal Accessibility: Built with large, high-contrast typography (Fredoka), text labels paired with every icon (avoiding ambiguous emojis), a mute toggle, a reduced-motion mode, and automatic on-screen touch controls (virtual joystick and action button) for tablets and smartphones.
  • Classroom & Hardware Resilience: Includes a ?canvas URL parameter to switch to a lightweight renderer for older school computers, plus a sub-one-minute interactive tutorial so students can start playing immediately.
  • Data Reliability & Transparency: Because NASA’s shared DEMO_KEY has strict hourly rate limits, the game caches live API responses in the browser for 6 hours and includes a saved snapshot of real DONKI records for offline play. The title screen and in-game NASA Archives terminal always transparently display whether data is LIVE, a SAVED COPY, or a saved sample.

Tools, Languages, Data & Software Stack

  • Languages & Core Web Technologies: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6+), JSON, and browser LocalStorage (for high scores, badges, Field Journal progress, and API caching).
  • Game Engine & Assets: Phaser 3 (2D game framework), custom procedural map rendering (scenery.js), Kenney "Sci-Fi RTS" sprites (CC0), Phosphor Icons (MIT), and Fredoka font (SIL OFL).
  • NASA Data & Scientific References: NASA Open APIs (DONKI CME, GST, FLR, and SEP endpoints), NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR)-inspired biological scenarios, and NASA Mars Exploration / Artemis mission parameters.
  • Development & Deployment Tools: Visual Studio Code, Git/GitHub, Python (http.server for local testing), GitHub Pages with custom domain routing (missionmars.games via Name.com DNS), and Claude Code (used as an AI coding assistant to help implement and debug the JavaScript/Phaser codebase alongside our team's game design, balancing, and NASA data integration).
